contexts: Consistent with Signaling Theory (Spence, 1973) and Serna’s (2020) integrated framework, university tiers in Vietnam function as an aggregated “signal package” conveying informa - tion about institutional quality, selectivity, and expected student performance.
By structur - ing our predictor selection in this way, we ensured that the quantitative analysis directly embodies the dual theoretical foundations of Signaling Theory and Identity Economics.

Through the lens of Signaling Theory and Identity Economics (Serna, 2020), the study examines how institutional messages, personal identity, and social and economic factors shape students’ decisions in Vietnam’s test-based, tiered higher education system.

When institutional signals meet student identity, they create an interpretive space, which also represents the intersection point between Signaling Theory and Identity Economics in Serna’s integrated framework.

To establish a robust conceptual foundation, our study draws on two complementary theo - retical perspectives: Signaling Theory and Identity Economics, following the integrated approach proposed by Serna (2020).
The framework also shaped our interpretation of the data, allowing us to contextualize students’ decisions within the broader theoretical per - spectives of Signaling Theory and Identity Economics.

Drawing on Signaling Theory and Identity Economics framework (Serna, 2020), the study explores how institutional signals, family expectations, and social identity shape their educational pathways within a tier-based higher education structure.

Signaling Theory, introduced by Spence (1973 ), provides a framework for understanding how individuals and institutions convey information about quality and ability through observable indicators or “signals.”
Aligning with Signaling Theory, Vietnamese universities rely heavily on measurable indicators such as entrance exam score thresholds to convey selectivity and prestige (Serna, 2020).
